fact: WHO Madagascar reports that nutrition and maternal health were integrated into DHIS2, which it calls the national electronic health information management system, and that completeness of the SRMNIA-nutrition data rose from 53% in 2023 to 85% in 2025 (source given as DHIS2, DEPSI/MSANP).

WHO Madagascar lists, as key actions of the 2024-2025 biennium, modernisation of the DHIS2 platform (an audit and secured Cloud hosting, reported as in place), deployment of electronic registers including the Rapport Mensuel d'Activité, and distribution of tablets with training on DHIS2; it gives no counts of facilities.

WHO Madagascar reports that the data quality score in the district referral hospitals (CHRD) fell to 31% against a target of 85% for 2024/2025, on supervision reports, in its table of SIS and DHIS2 indicators.

WHO Madagascar states that the country updated its governing framework for health data and information through the Plan Stratégique de Santé Numérique 2023-2027 (held by DEPSI, update reported 100% complete), with a SCORE 2025 assessment and an overall SIS architecture developed with USAID support.

WHO Madagascar's indicator tables for 2023-2025 cite their source as DHIS2, DEPSI/MSANP, placing the platform's data with the health ministry's DEPSI directorate; the report does not otherwise state who operates the platform.

fact: A 2021 malaria data quality assessment of 30 health centres in Atsinanana (14 of 52) and Atsimo-Andrefana (16 of 65), published in AJTMH, describes health centres compiling HMIS monthly summary reports from registers on standard reporting forms and submitting them to the health district by the 15th of the following month, with DHIS2 data checked as a separate, third source; it does not say in terms who keys the DHIS2 entry.

The 2021 assessment (AJTMH) found monthly report submission completeness of 100% and timeliness of 85% (Atsinanana) and 95% (Atsimo-Andrefana) among the 30 health centres assessed in two of 22 health regions, a convenience sample of centres whose 2021 timeliness was below 70%; data-element completeness was 43% and 68%.

The 2021 assessment (AJTMH) names the health centres' primary documents for recording patient information as the outpatient register, laboratory register, pharmacy dispensing log and stock logs, scoring the reserve stock of registers or reporting forms at 43% (Atsinanana) and 64% (Atsimo-Andrefana) across 30 health centres; it names no electronic patient record.

fact: The health ministry's PSRSIS 2023-2027 states that management of the health information system is assigned to two MSANP directorates, DEPSI for routine data and DVSSER for surveillance data, and that MSANP adopted DHIS2 as its data warehouse under the 2018-2022 plan, with a DHIS2 task force of ministry trainers and technicians; no date is given for the position, so the published date is used.

MSANP's Plan Stratégique de Renforcement du Système d'Information Sanitaire runs 2023-2027, carries a costed budget by strategy, and names DHIS2 throughout, including a DHIS2 improvement plan, scale-up of the electronic RMA and an objective of at least 95% timeliness and completeness of reports from all facilities by 2027.

The PSRSIS reports the December 2022 national SIS forum's finding that the absence of autonomous financing and poor pooling of partners' resources are a major bottleneck, and that 34.69% of the previous plan's activities were under way with partners' contributions; the State budget share allocated to the SIS has no 2022 baseline (ND) against a 4% target for 2023.

The PSRSIS (DEPSI) states that DHIS2 was scaled to all 22 regions and 114 districts in January 2019 for the basic health centres' monthly activity report (RMA CSB), that the district hospital (CHRD, private sector included) and community RMAs were integrated from July 2020, and that DHIS2 is already used to collect CHRD data, while the CHU/CHRR/ES report was last updated in 2011 and DHIS2 is only to be brought forward for it; 50% of CSB had coherent data in DHIS2 at the 2022 baseline. The position is as at the plan, so the published date is used.

The PSRSIS states that data from the basic health centres (CSB) go up to the districts on the integrated RMA in paper form, which is keyed into the DHIS2 Routine platform; no date is given, so the published date is used.

The PSRSIS states that an electronic RMA keyed directly at health facilities has been piloted since 2021 (January 2021 in the text, October 2021 in the DHIS2 timeline, in Manjakandriana and Andramasina) and is available in 10 pilot districts (Andramasina, Manjakandriana, Manakara, Tuléar II, Nosy Varika, Ikongo, Vohipeno, Fandriana, Ambohimahasoa, Mananjary), with scale-up being planned; it gives no count of facilities.

The PSRSIS 2023-2027 lists as activities to develop a patient management and electronic reporting system for all care structures (CSB, CHRD) and a reporting and patient management platform for the CHU/CHR/ES, and says DEPSI and DGFS envisage a standard patient management tool interoperable with DHIS2; it says hospital data management has had no development programme of its own.

2424.mg reports that the hospital digitalisation project was initiated by the digital development ministry (MNDPT), which held a working meeting on its implementation at its Digital Center with officials of the Ministry of Public Health; its stated priorities include patient-flow management, traceability of medical records and transparency of services. The meeting is dated only as 'this Friday', so the published date is used.

2424.mg reports that two pilot sites were chosen to start the hospital digitalisation project, the Centre hospitalier universitaire Ravoahangy Andrianavalona and the CHU de soins et de santé publique at Analakely (CHUSSPA); the article reports the choice of sites and a planning meeting, not a system in use. No date is given beyond 'this Friday', so the published date is used.

The AMC-MAD congress report on Datasanté's site states that, at the cyber-health round table of 5 November 2024 attended by the health ministry (DGFS) and DEPSI, the electronic personal medical record was described as functional in some private establishments and some basic health centres (CSB), with technical and financial obstacles slowing implementation at scale; no figures are given.
The AMC-MAD congress report says the electronic medical record works in 'certain' private establishments and CSB as at the round table of 5 November 2024 and gives no count or share of facilities.

The congress report states that the computerised patient record software used in Madagascar's community medical centres is Datasanté's, that the Datasanté team trained practitioners on it and on the DATABOX on 7 November 2024, and that AMC-MAD (the community doctors' association) and Datasanté signed a convention on 6 November 2024 continuing their partnership and extending the network of front-line doctors using it.

The congress report states that the convention signed on 6 November 2024 between AMC-MAD and Datasanté provides for Datasanté's continued logistical and financial support; no state funding of the patient record software is mentioned, and the round table called for more support from the ministry.

The health ministry's national digital health strategy states that DHIS-2 is the single platform the Ministry adopted to support the health information system, that DEPSI leads coordination of digital health starting with the SIS, and that DEPSI alone holds a secured datacentre, used for the SIS only; the HMIS work was initiated in 2015-2016. The position is as at the strategy's imprint of January 2023.

The Stratégie Nationale de Santé Digitale 2023-2027, issued by the Ministry of Public Health in January 2023 to replace the 2016-2019 strategy that lapsed at the end of 2019, names DHIS-2 as the ministry's single HMIS platform and carries an estimated budget by activity, including USD 8.1 million (34.83 billion Ariary) to digitalise priority health services.

The strategy states that the budget allocated to digital health is minimal and goes essentially to consumables, and that digital health interventions are financed essentially by partners' support (equipment, internet connection, support services, training); the share of the State budget allocated to digital health has no 2022 baseline (ND) against a 1% target for 2023. The statement covers digital health as a whole, the HMIS being its longest-running part.

The ministry's strategy states that management of clinical data and of the hospital information system remains at an experimental and local stage, and cites the WHO Africa Region digital health survey as reporting a few pilot initiatives using electronic health records; it adds that patient-management applications are used in private practices and private health centres. It gives no count and does not say at which tier the experiments run.

fact: On Datasanté's page a community doctor at Matielona, sole general practitioner for about 12,000 people, states that since using a tablet linked by wifi to her solar-powered Datasantébox she keeps no paper register and everything is in each patient's computerised record, held on the local server; she received the equipment in November 2019 and speaks after several years of use. The page is undated, so the published date is used.

A study presented by Dr Diamondra Mandimbimalala on Datasanté's page covers 35 community doctors (25 private, 10 public) trained and equipped with Datasanté: 10 use the software regularly and 20 irregularly; 12 have created more than 1,000 patient records, 6 between 500 and 1,000, and 12 fewer than 500. The count is of doctors, not facilities, there is no denominator, and the study is undated, so the published date is used.

Datasanté's page describes the software as used by community general practitioners, first-line doctors in isolated rural practice, 25 of the 35 equipped being private and 10 public; it says the 2019 server-client version will also be offered to public basic health centres (CSB), which is a proposal and not a deployment. The page is undated, so the published date is used.

Datasanté's page presents the network as run by Datasanté with the community doctors' association AMC-MAD, a volunteer pilot programme dating from early 2010 with equipment handed to doctors in full ownership; among the study's perspectives is to conclude an agreement with the health ministry, which implies none existed. The page is undated, so the published date is used.

Datasanté's page states that it is seeking partnerships between actors of the North and Malagasy general practitioners to finance the equipment (Datasantébox server, battery, tablet, mobile solar panel), supplied to participating doctors without per diem; no state funding is mentioned. The plan is described as for 2019.
